title: Cutting-Edge Deep Learning Techniques in Plant Disease Detection: A Systematic Review
abstract: The developments in deep learning have greatly influenced the processes of the identification of plant diseases, producing outstanding enhancements in terms of precision and functionality. The aims of this survey are to provide a comprehensive literature review of deep learning techniques in plant disease diagnosis and prognosis with special emphasis on recent development and future developments for further study. It provides critical analysis of the most popular models including CNNs, Transfer Learning, Few-Shot Learning and shares insights on how these technologies are applied in crops including rice, wheat and maize. These challenges include the lack of quality data, and the problem of transferring models from one environment to another, as well as the computational complexity that makes the application of these models in agriculture. Moreover, the investigation identifies the IoT and Edge Computing as a potential for the early disease diagnosis and surveillance. The paper also points out that the significance of Explainable AI or XAI is taking firm root; this is an innovation that seeks to explain the workings of models; thus, making it popular among stakeholders in agriculture. This literature from the last decade is analyzed to outline the research priorities and possibilities for future development in the design of new models, ways of sharing data, and ongoing field evaluation. This survey is to be used by the researchers and practitioners who are involved in developing sustainable and scalable approaches of managing plant diseases using deep learning technology.
venue: 2024 4th International Conference on Ubiquitous Computing and Intelligent Information Systems (ICUIS)

title: High-Accuracy Maize Disease Detection Based on Attention Generative Adversarial Network and Few-Shot Learning
abstract: This study addresses the problem of maize disease detection in agricultural production, proposing a high-accuracy detection method based on Attention Generative Adversarial Network (Attention-GAN) and few-shot learning. The method introduces an attention mechanism, enabling the model to focus more on the significant parts of the image, thereby enhancing model performance. Concurrently, data augmentation is performed through Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to generate more training samples, overcoming the difficulties of few-shot learning. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses other baseline models in accuracy, recall, and mean average precision (mAP), achieving 0.97, 0.92, and 0.95, respectively. These results validate the high accuracy and stability of the method in handling maize disease detection tasks. This research provides a new approach to solving the problem of few samples in practical applications and offers valuable references for subsequent research, contributing to the advancement of agricultural informatization and intelligence.

title: Few-shot canine disease detection using transfer learning with two-stage fine-tuning on YOLO
abstract: In veterinary medicine, deep learning for automatic canine disease detection is receiving increasing interest. Most existing approaches are based on conventional supervised learning. These methods require large and well-balanced datasets. As a result, they show limited adaptability when only a small number of labeled samples are available. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a few-shot object detection framework based on a two-stage fine-tuning approach integrated into the YOLOv11 model. The proposed approach first learns robust and transferable features from base disease classes. It then adapts to novel disease classes using only a small number of labeled samples by fine-tuning the detection head. We carried out thorough experiments on a veterinary dataset. In total, nine disease categories are considered, where seven base classes are used for training and two novel classes are reserved for few-shot evaluation. Based on the experiments, the proposed method exceeds conventional YOLO-based transfer learning in performance. In the 15-shot scenario, the model attains an mAP@50 of 0.985. It also demonstrates strong stability, showing a standard deviation of just 0.007 across ten separate tasks. Overall, these findings suggest that the proposed model offers a practical, stable, and cost-effective solution for canine disease detection under limited data conditions within a consistent imaging domain.

title: Comparative Analysis of Coconut Disease Using EfficientNet and Few-Shot Transfer Learning
abstract: Coconut cultivation plays a vital role in tropical agriculture and contributes significantly to food security and economic sustainability. However, coconut production is increasingly threatened by various leaf, stem, and fruit diseases that reduce yield and quality, posing challenges to farmers and stakeholders. Traditional disease detection methods rely heavily on manual inspection, which is time-consuming, prone to human error, and impractical for large-scale monitoring. Recent advances in deep learning have shown potential in plant disease recognition, yet existing models demand extensive annotated datasets, which are often scarce for coconut-specific diseases. To address this limitation, this study proposes a Comparative Analysis of Coconut Disease using EfficientNet with Few-Shot Transfer Learning (CAEFTL) framework, which leverages the feature extraction efficiency of EfficientNet and the adaptability of few-shot learning to improve classification accuracy with limited training samples. Experimental evaluations were conducted on a curated coconut disease dataset, where the CAEFTL approach achieved superior performance compared to baseline convolutional neural networks, recording an accuracy of 97.8%, precision of 96.5%, and F1-score of 97.1%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining EfficientNet’s lightweight architecture with few-shot transfer learning to overcome data scarcity challenges. In conclusion, the proposed CA-EFTL model provides an efficient, scalable, and accurate solution for coconut disease detection, offering valuable implications for precision agriculture and digital farming practices in resource-constrained environments.
venue: 2025 International Conference on Decision Aid Sciences and Applications (DASA)

title: A Novel Ensemble Loss Function of Few-Shot Learning for Tomato Leaf Disease Detection
abstract: This study explores the use of various loss functions, such as Quadratic Loss, Hinge loss, Ll loss, KL divergence loss, and Huber loss, for detecting tomato leaf diseases in Few-Shot Learning (FSL) models. The goal is to create a flexible FSL model that accurately categorizes tomato leaf diseases using a limited number of annotated instances. The authors assess the effectiveness of each loss function separately on datasets of tomato, grapes, apple, and maize leaves. They propose a new method of combining loss functions using exponential transformation to maximize the advantages of each loss function while minimizing their disadvantages. This integrated strategy aims to improve the FSL model's ability to differentiate between healthy and sick leaves. The authors examined five distinct loss functions and combined them using an exponential transformation technique. The results show that the proposed FSL model, which incorporates exponential loss functions, achieves outstanding performance in tasks related to detecting diseases in tomato leaves. This novel strategy is expected to enhance the model's ability to distinguish between healthy and diseased leaves, improving overall disease detection capabilities.
venue: 2024 10th International Conference on Advanced Computing and Communication Systems (ICACCS)

title: Few-Shot Transfer Learning for Pneumonia Detection From Chest X-Ray Images
abstract: The availability of large, high-quality annotated datasets remains one of the primary challenges in medical image analysis, particularly for chest X-ray interpretation, where expert annotation is costly and time-consuming. Although deep learning methods, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have demonstrated strong performance in thoracic disease detection, their effectiveness typically depends on large-scale labeled data, which are often unavailable in real-world clinical settings. Fewshot learning addresses this challenge by enabling models to adapt to new tasks using only a very limited number of labeled samples. In medical imaging, transfer-based few-shot learning-where pre-trained models are fine-tuned using limited labeled medical data-has emerged as a practical alternative to metalearning approaches that require task distributions rarely accessible in healthcare scenarios. This paper presents a controlled evaluation of transfer-based few-shot learning pipelines for pneumonia detection from chest X-ray images. Four widely used CNN architectures-CheXNet, ResNet50, EfficientNet-B0, and DenseNet121—are evaluated under identical experimental conditions using 1 -shot, 5 -shot, and 10 -shot learning scenarios. The evaluation protocol incorporates five-fold cross-validation and statistical comparison across architectures. Experimental results in the 5 -shot setting show that all four architectures achieve competitive performance, with DenseNet121 attaining the highest F1-score of 91.5%, ResNet50 achieving the highest accuracy of 88.1%, and EfficientNet-B0 demonstrating strong recall of 91.6% following class-weighted training. CheXNet achieves an F1-score of 87.0%, confirming that ImageNet-initialized architectures are competitive with domain-specific pre-training under extreme data scarcity. The findings highlight the importance of dense feature reuse, partial backbone fine-tuning, and loss calibration in data-scarce medical imaging tasks, providing practical guidance for selecting deep learning backbones in clinical environments where large annotated datasets are unavailable. An ablation study on DenseNet121 under the 10-shot protocol reveals that partial backbone fine-tuning is the single most critical component, with freezing the backbone causing a 22 pp accuracy drop, while augmentation contributes minimally in the extreme few-shot regime.
venue: 2026 IEEE 6th International Conference on Smart Information Systems and Technologies (SIST)

title: Optimization of matching networks with transfer learning in few-shot pneumonia detection
abstract: Pneumonia remains a leading cause of death among children under five years of age, with approximately 1.6 million fatalities annually, especially in low-resource settings where diagnostic capacity is limited. Early detection plays a critical role in reducing pneumonia-related mortality; however, most traditional diagnostic methods depend heavily on trained personnel and medical infrastructure, which are often lacking in underserved areas. While machine learning has emerged as a promising approach for automating diagnosis, existing models typically rely on large volumes of annotated data, making them less applicable in real-world clinical scenarios where labeled data is scarce. To address this gap, we propose a hybrid model that combines transfer learning with few-shot learning, using MobileNetV3 as a lightweight feature extractor and Matching Networks for classification based on limited labeled examples. This integration is designed to improve both data efficiency and diagnostic accuracy. The key novelty of this work lies in the fusion of pre-trained deep representations with a metric-learning framework to enable effective pneumonia detection under one-shot or few-shot conditions. The model was evaluated on a publicly available, balanced chest X-ray dataset involving three classes: COVID-19, pneumonia, and normal. Experimental results demonstrated high classification performance, with an accuracy of 93.21%, precision of 93.34%, recall of 93.20%, and F1-score of 93.19%. The proposed model also achieved AUCs of 1.00 for COVID and 0.98 for both pneumonia and normal cases, outperforming traditional machine learning baselines such as Random Forest and Support Vector Machines. An ablation study was conducted to isolate the contributions of each component, confirming that the performance gains are attributable to the integration of MobileNetV3 and Matching Networks. Although external validation was not included in this study, the architecture was designed with adaptability in mind, making it a promising candidate for deployment in real-world, resource-constrained healthcare environments and future expansion to new disease categories. The proposed model achieved 93.21% accuracy, effectively detecting pneumonia with limited labeled data. MobileNetV3 and Matching Networks ensured efficient classification, ideal for resource-constrained settings. High AUC scores (1.0 for COVID, 0.98 for normal/pneumonia) highlight model reliability in real-world diagnostics.

title: Few-Shot Fruit Segmentation via Transfer Learning
abstract: Advancements in machine learning, computer vision, and robotics have paved the way for transformative solutions in various domains, particularly in agriculture. For example, accurate identification and segmentation of fruits from field images plays a crucial role in automating jobs such as harvesting, disease detection, and yield estimation. However, achieving robust and precise infield fruit segmentation remains a challenging task since large amounts of labeled data are required to handle variations in fruit size, shape, color, and occlusion. In this paper, we develop a few-shot semantic segmentation framework for infield fruits using transfer learning. Concretely, our work is aimed at addressing agricultural domains that lack publicly available labeled data. Motivated by similar success in urban scene parsing, we propose specialized pre-training using a public benchmark dataset for fruit transfer learning. By leveraging pre-trained neural networks, accurate semantic segmentation of fruit in the field is achieved with only a few labeled images. Furthermore, we show that models with pre-training learn to distinguish between fruit still on the trees and fruit that have fallen on the ground, and they can effectively transfer the knowledge to the target fruit dataset.
venue: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation

title: Comparative Analysis of Few-Shot Learning and Transfer Learning for Medical Imaging Tumour Classification
abstract: Prostate cancer is the second most common disease in men in the United States and touches the lives of millions of men every year, thereby becoming an important global health issue. The glandular prostate (PG), which plays a pivotal role in seminal fluid production, is the main organ that gets targeted by this disease. Since magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is not invasive and gives accurate soft-tissue contrast, it has become an essential diagnostic tool for prostate cancer. To enhance the accuracy and efficacy of prostate cancer detection from MRI images, we present in this paper an improved deep learning approach that employs the InceptionResNetV2 model and exploits transfer learning. Compared with traditional diagnosis approaches, our model is effective in extracting intricate features and enhancing sensitivity. We also explore the viability of few-shot learning in medical imaging using prototypical networks with a minor portion of the dataset and reveal the potential of few-shot learning strategies in cases with limited annotated medical images and lay the groundwork for future studies. Large-scale validation shows strong and stable results, endorsing the applicability of our method in clinical environments for early detection and tailored treatment planning, eventually leading to enhanced patient outcomes.
venue: 2026 International Conference on Signal Processing and Electronics Design (ICSPED)

title: Cross-Lingual Alzheimer’s Disease Speech Detection: Polarity Inversion and Few-Shot Calibration Strategies
abstract: Speech-based non-invasive screening offers a cost-effective and scalable approach for the early detection of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, the clinical utility of deep learning models remains severely constrained by the scarcity of labeled speech data in low-resource languages, necessitating cross-lingual transfer learning. Conventional domain adaptation paradigms typically assume semantically consistent feature domains and focus heavily on aligning marginal distributions; however, they suffer catastrophic performance degradation when applied to cross-lingual pathologic speech. By analyzing disease-associated representation vectors within a self-supervised HuBERT space, we uncover a systematic mechanism driving this failure, a phenomenon we term cross-lingual polarity flip, where the direction of disease-relative-to-control feature offsets fundamentally reverses between languages. While prior multilingual studies have largely discarded such dimensional inconsistencies as ungeneralizable noise, a 500-round Monte Carlo stability analysis demonstrates that these flips occur in a highly stable, structural manner across 18.3% of top discriminative dimensions. Leveraging this insight, we introduce Monte Carlo Polarity Flip Calibration (MC-PFC), a few-shot framework designed to explicitly rectify flip orientations. Requiring only five labeled support samples per class from the target domain, MC-PFC robustly estimates direction flips via a separability-weighted ensemble voting mechanism. Evaluated on a strictly held-out Chinese blind test set, MC-PFC achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.871, recovering 99.5% of the performance achieved by a full in-domain trained upper bound (AUC = 0.875). Ablation experiments confirm that direction calibration yields a substantial +0.361 AUC gain, vastly outperforming standard distribution alignment (+0.081). This work establishes a data-efficient paradigm for cross-lingual medical analysis, shifting the clinical AI focus from discarding cross-lingual discrepancies to actively modeling and calibrating them.

title: Optimizing Few-Shot Learning via Reptile Meta-Learning Approach for Toxoplasmosis Chorioretinitis Detection
abstract: Few-shot learning has emerged as a viable paradigm for addressing learning problems with minimal labeled instances, with recurrent issues such as overfitting and intricate feature extraction posing challenges that limit its effectiveness across various fields. In our study, we present a meta-learning technique that uses the Reptile algorithm to diagnose toxoplasmosis chorioretini-tis. Our approach capitalizes transfer learning, using cutting-edge Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures-ResNet50, VGG-16, and Inception V3 as foundational models. Using the reptile meta-learning technique, we painstakingly test and compare these models' performance in diagnosing toxoplasmosis retinitis. This study represents an important step forward in the expanding field of meta-learning approaches for medical image classification as it adapts to tasks where the data is minimal, especially in the medical field where collection of large labeled data is difficult. It highlights Reptile's adaptability to the complexities inherent in ocular disease datasets, demonstrating its potential to significantly improve disease classification accuracy across a variety of medical imaging tasks. The proposed methodology emerges as a potent tool. In our evaluations, VGG-16 had an accuracy of 66%, ResNet50 had an accuracy of 80%, and Inception V3 had an accuracy of 84%. These findings not only support the usefulness of our technique but also demonstrate Inception V3's superior performance in distinguishing toxoplasmosis retinitis within the field of ocular illness detection.

title: A deep learning model for detection and classification of coffee-leaf diseases using the transfer-learning technique
abstract: The early treatment  and detection of plant diseases are important processes, as many diseases affecting crops are highly contagious. Recent advancements in deep learning have helped to provide innovative tools that have not only assisted early detection, but also significantly improved the performance and accuracy of Coffee Leaf Disease (CLD) classification and treatment. However, training a deep learning model from scratch can be both resource and time-consuming. To overcome this challenge, the transfer learning technique can take full advantage of pre-trained  models for more general tasks on extensive datasets o ameliorate the performance of a new, related task using few-shot training. This paper proposes a deep learning model, coupled with transfer learning, for CLD detection that aims to provide high accuracy forecasting of diseases that could affect coffee leaves. Our method involves 195 different pre-trained deep learning models, including real-time models like MobileNet and dense ones like EfficientNet and ResNet for the detection of four different diseases. The findings suggest that the EfficientNetB0 model, with transfer learning, has the most relevent accuracy (99.99%), and thus offers an effective solution for coffee leaf diseases classification of. This result could be used to develop applications that help coffee growers to improve the productivity and quality of their crops through early and accurate detection of coffee plant leaf diseases. Such an Artificial Intelligence based application would provide growers with timely control measures, preventing the spread of disease, and minimizing crop damage.
venue: International Journal of Advances in Intelligent Informatics

title: Enhancing Approaches to Detect Papilloma-Associated Hyperostosis Using a Few-Shot Transfer Learning Framework in Extremely Scarce Radiological Datasets
abstract: Background/Objectives: The application of deep learning models for rare diseases faces significant difficulties due to severe data scarcity. The detection of focal hyperostosis (PAH) is a crucial radiological sign for the surgical planning of sinonasal inverted papilloma, yet data is often limited. This study introduces and validates a robust methodological framework for building clinically meaningful deep learning models under extremely limited data conditions (n = 20). Methods: We propose a few-shot learning framework based on the nnU-Net architecture, which integrates an in-domain transfer learning strategy (fine-tuning a pre-trained skull segmentation model) to address data scarcity. To further enhance robustness, a specialized data augmentation technique called “window shifting” is introduced to simulate inter-scanner variability. The entire framework was evaluated using a rigorous 5-fold cross-validation strategy. Results: Our proposed framework achieved a stable mean Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.48 ± 0.06. This performance significantly outperformed a baseline model trained from scratch, which failed to converge and yielded a clinically insignificant mean DSC of 0.09 ± 0.02. Conclusions: The analysis demonstrates that this methodological approach effectively overcomes instability and overfitting, generating reproducible and valuable predictions suitable for rare data types where large-scale data collection is not feasible.

title: Enhancing Dermatological Diagnosis with Few-Shot Learning
abstract: Automated skin disease classification poses significant challenges due to limited labeled dermatological data and class imbalance. This study proposes a deep learning-based system that leverages Few-Shot Learning (FSL) to enhance multiskin disease detection, focusing on Vitiligo, Seborrheic Keratosis, and Eczema. Utilizing a 3 -way N -shot learning approach, we assess the performance of VGG19, ResNet50, and DenseNet121 under 5 -shot, 7 -shot, and 10 -shot settings. Experimental results indicate that DenseNet121 achieves the highest accuracy of 96.66% and an F1-score of 0.97 in the 10- shot configuration, demonstrating its superior generalization. ResNet50 shows robust performance in the 5 -shot setting (93.33% accuracy, 0.92 F1score) but drops to 83.33% accuracy and 0.85 F1-score in the 10 -shot scenario, suggesting sensitivity to data volume. VGG19 lags behind, with a peak accuracy of 73.66% and an F1-score of 0.75. Incorporating attention mechanisms after each pretrained model further improves classification accuracy and F1-scores, demonstrating the effectiveness of FSL combined with transfer learning in dermatological applications, making it a viable AIassisted diagnostic tool for low-resource clinical settings.
venue: International Conference on Computing Communication Control and automation
